messages.subject_clean: Postdoctoral Associate: morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods
messages.body_plain:
Postdoctoral Associate: morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods

The Adams laboratory, Department of Ecology, Evolution and Organismal Biology (EEOB) at Iowa State University, is seeking applicants for a fulltime postdoctoral position in geometric morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods. This position is for a maximum of two years and is part of an NSF collaborative CIBR project. The postdoctoral associate will contribute to ongoing macroevolutionary studies in vertebrates, will coordinate the development of tutorials and code profiling in geomorph, and will mentor undergraduates in quantitative morphology studies. Successful applicants are encouraged to develop their own independent empirical research in multivariate macroevolution.

Additional details about the position, as well as a link to apply, may be found on the ISU HR website:https://isu.wd1.myworkdayjobs.com/IowaStateJobs/job/Ames-IA/Postdoctoral-Research-Associate---Ecology--Evolution-and-Organismal-Biology_R1519

Questions about the position should be directed to Dean Adams (dca...@iastate.edu).

Dean

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Iowa State University

messages.subject: change x axis scale for CR modularity plot (and a bonus question)
messages.subject_clean: change x axis scale for CR modularity plot (and a bonus question)
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

Question 1. I ran some data in the modularity test. I plotted the results using this code.

APF.mod <- modularity.test(APTM.gpa$coords, land.gps, iter=999, print.progress = FALSE)
plot(APF.mod)

The plot gives me what appears to be a standard scale on the x-axis of 0.0-2.0 (attached Rplot03). But it is basically unreadable.

 I tried to modify it using this code (and other variations), but I can't modify it.

plot(APF.mod, xlim=c(0.8,1.2))

Is there a way to modify the plot for publication or illustration?

Question 2. As I was fiddling around with the code, I changed the iterations from 999 to 9999.
 The 999 iterations produced a CR of 0.9685 and a p-value of 0.002. Seems reasonable.

But the 9999 iterations produced a CR of 0.96855 (seems OK, but shouldn't the 999 CR round up to 0.9686?), but a p-value of 8E-04. The results are illustrated on top of the plot, where the p-value is listed as 0.000800000000000023 (attached).

The p-value seems incorrect in several ways. It doesn't round up to 0.002, it shouldn't have calculated more than 4 decimal places.
What's going on?

Dave Thulman

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] change x axis scale for CR modularity plot (and a bonus question)
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] change x axis scale for CR modularity plot (and a bonus question)
messages.body_plain:
Dave,

For the plot, you will need to grab the permutation outputs. Try this:

hist(APF.mod$random.CR,xlim = c(0.8, 1.2))

As to using 999 vs 9999 iterations, a few comments for clarity. Yes, the observed value (up to rounding error) should be the same. However, the p-value, while close, will not be identical, as each permutation schedule will differ slightly. What one will find however, is that as you increase the number of permutations, the variance in p-values across multiple runs will decrease (I showed this back in 1995 for a permutational anova).  It turns out that this is a well-known property of permutation methods, that increasing the number of iterations will cause things to converge on a more precise p-value.

Finally, yes, for 9999 the significance level should only have 4 digits. That is a plotting error. Thanks for bringing it to our attention.

Hope this helps.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

messages.subject: Interpreting integration and modularity results
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,
I have been working on an archaeology problem involving chipped  stone spear points. These can best be conceptualized as analogous to a knife, which has a handle and a blade. Through the life of the knife, the blade is repeatedly resharpened and both its size and shape changes, while the handle generally stays the same size and shape.

We divided the handle module from the blade module on 100 of the spear points. I analyzed them using integration.test and modularity.test in Geomorph. As suspected the modularity test was highly significant (CR = 0.9685, p = .002) , but unexpectedly so was the integration test (r-PLS: 0.928, p = 0.001).

>From my course notes and reading several pubs, it seems the two tests should be complementary in the sense that if you find strong modularity, you should also find weak integration and vice versa.

I suspect that I am misunderstanding what integration actually is. Modularity seems clear: high covariation within in the modules and low covariation between the modules. Does Integration mean that as one module changes size, the other does also? I could see that as the blades are resharpened their relative size changes (gets smaller) in relation to the handle size.

A potential confounding factor in these data is that the handle sizes (and shapes) are not uniform. It may be that there are really 2 or more different spear point types in the dataset.

Any help in conceptualizing this result is appreciated.

Dave Thulman

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Interpreting integration and modularity results
messages.body_plain:
Dave,

This is a common misconception, that is unfortunately perpetuated in the literature, and based largely on the use of the RV coefficient.  The reason for this misconception is that the RV was proposed for testing both integration and for testing modularity. Recall that the RV ranges from 0 à 1, with higher values represented greater between-module covariation, and values closer to zero mean less between-module covariation. That has (incorrectly) been set up as a conceptual dichotomy (or gradient) between modularity on one hand and integration on the other (see my 2016 paper for some discussion of this issue).

However, there are multiple problems with this perspective. First, as a thought experiment, if low RV = modularity, and high RV = integration, what value represents neither?  In other words, if these are two ends of a continuum, what is the null hypothesis against which they both are compared?  There isn’t one.

Second, we know that expected values of RV (for random data) change with both N and p (see figures in the above paper). That means that how ‘modular’ or how ‘integrated’ some structure is depends on sample size and the number of variables: it is not an intrinsic measure. Therefore, even if one could come up with a null RV value that represents neither integration nor modularity, that value would have to be on a shifting scale with N and p.  Simply not tractable.

Third, the permutation test for evaluating RV for integration is different in implementation than it is for evaluating modularity using the RV. For modularity, we ask whether the covariation between modules RELATIVE to covariation within modules is less than expected from a random combination of modules. This is evaluated by a permutation of columns (variables). For integration, we ask whether there is greater covariation between modules than expected by random association of modules . This test does not mention anything about the within-module covariation, and is evaluated by shuffling the rows (objects) of one module while leaving the other module the same.  So from a statistical testing standpoint, there really is not a single continuum; one is just using the same summary measure (RV) for two distinct biological and statistical tests.

Because of this, it is empirically possible to have both modularity and integration in the same dataset. This gets back to the fact that there are, actually, testing distinct null hypotheses for each of these tests, and they are not mutually exclusive. This appears to be what you have found in your dataset.

Dean

messages.subject: Too much choices.
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

Would you mind to help me to choose what should I apply to analyze a morphological disparity of my data? I have the number of shells with just 1 factor - different locations. Here are the options:

1. Morphological disparity for entire data set (why do I need it at all?)

2. Morphological disparity for entire data set, accounting for allometry (I didn't planned to study an allometry)

3. Morphological disparity without covariates, using overall mean (Hm...)

4. Morphological partial disparities for overal mean (...?)

5. Morphological disparity without covariates, using group means (o_O)

6. Morphological disparity of different groups than those described by the linear model (-_-)

Probably, the question is stupid, but a book with an answer cost too much for a student from a not developed country. Sci-hud didn't help either :)
I applied all variations of function and got TOTALLY different results.

Thank you in advance and Best wishes,
Lyna

messages.subject: Help with new version (>3.1.0)
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I've been away from morphometric studies for some time. Now, I have to redo some analyzes but it seems things have changed. I'd appreciate it if anyone can help me.

I have a data set with two factors: population and sex. I want to test if there is a difference in shape between populations or sexes (females are bigger than males so I am not sure how to handle this). It is an unbalanced study with different number of samples for different populations and differente male:female ratios therefore I opted for type II anova.

First, I check whether there is allometry:

fit.size <- procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize), SS.type = "II", data = elytra.gdf)
anova(fit.size)

Then I compare models with increasing complexity using the anova function and conclude "coords ~ log(Csize) * Site/Sex" is the better model ("coords ~ log(Csize) * Site * Sex" doesn't provide a significant change).

Then I test for the homogeneity of the allometry slopes between populations.

fit.common <- procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize) + Site / Sex, data = elytra.gdf, SS.type = "II")
fit.unique <- procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize) * Site / Sex, data = elytra.gdf, SS.type = "II")
anova(fit.common, fit.unique)

The result is insignificant so the slopes are homogeneous. Now I can do pairwise tests between sites for example, using log(csize) and sex as covariates.

fit.null <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + Sex, data = elytra.gdf, print.progress = FALSE, SS.type = "II")
fit.common <- procD.lm(f1 = coords ~ log(Csize) + treatment/family, data = elytra.gdf, SS.type = "II")
PW <- pairwise(fit.common, fit.null, groups = elytra.gdf$Site, print.progress = FALSE)
summary(PW, test.type = "dist", confidence = 0.95)

Is this the right way to approach in my case?

Thanks in advance!

One can have a factorial model, where there are species, and localities as main effects. The corresponding anova would then address whether species differ and whether localities differ (note: IF there is full representation of species in localities, the interaction term could also be examined for context-specific species differences across localities).

Following the anova, one could do pairwise comparisons to evaluate whether particular pairs of groups: species groups, locality groups, etc., differ from one another.

Again I suggest you consult the help files and vignettes of geomorph and RRPP. They provide examples of such analyses.

As to your species data, there appears to be some issue in reading your data into R.  That is not a geomorph problem, but an R I/O issue.

messages.body_plain:
One solution to this problem is to log-transform your size variable first, and place the log(Csize) in the geomorph data frame.  For instance:

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa,site = plethodon$site,species = plethodon$species, Csize2 = log(Csize2))

fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize2, data = gdf)

This is recommended in the vignette that accompanies RRPP: the package that is used to run the linear model for procD.lm.

I have tested an example with Csizes between 0 and 1, and performing things in this manner did work.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Burak,

The error produced is from lm.fit, a base R function, which is used within procD.lm.  We will have to investigate why this is happening.  I believe the problem is with the formation of the model frame lm.fit uses for the analysis.  If I try using lm.fit directly it works okay but within procD.lm (and the lm.rrpp function it uses), taking the log of centroid size produces NaN values.  Something is quirky here - might take some sleuthing to figure it out.

However, you are absolutely correct with you that you can add a constant.  The log transformation is really log(x + c) and it changes nothing for ANOVA statistics to vary c.  With c = 0 and all x < 1, you find your error.  I pumped c to 5 and 10 to verify and each time it worked, and ANOVA stats were consistent.

As Dean pointed out, you could also do the log-transformation first and add it to the data frame.  In R, data frames are converted to model frames based on the instructions in the formula.  This seems to be where the issue is, and Dean’s suggestion means not transforming a variable that has already been transformed.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with new version (>3.1.0)
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

As a follow up on this thread, I have identified the issue causing problems, and it is indeed an issue with building of model frames.  This issue only manifests with within-formula transformations, e.g.,

~ log(x)
~ploy(x, 2)

There is no issue if variables are not transformed.  I am updating code (in RRPP, not geomorph) and will send this to CRAN soon.  It will probably take a few days to be available on CRAN; a new version (patch) of RRPP will be available on github later today.  I normally would not preview that this is happening, rather than tell you once it happened, but I wish to warn you that until this is fixed, it is best to use Dean’s suggestion if you want to transform a variables for analysis.  For example, if you want to analyze procD.lm(coords ~ log(size), data = gdf), instead do this:

gdf$logsize <- log(gdf$size)
procD.lm(coords ~ logsize)

The reason I implore you to do this is that you might get ANOVA results that seem fine while the coefficients are incorrect.  The issue is not revealed with ANOVA, because the variance of the linear association stays the same, even though the slope changes, due to the model frame issue.  This could have consequences for downstream analyses, like comparing slopes.

Thanks to Burak for pointing out this stealthy mishap!  I will send out another message once we have it resolved.

Mike

messages.subject: A question about lm.rrpp?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

In the vignette using RRPP, second example demonstrates:

data(Pupfish)
Pupfish$logSize <- log(Pupfish$CS)
fit <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ logSize + Sex*Pop, SS.type = "I",
               data = Pupfish, print.progress = FALSE)
summary(fit, formula = FALSE)

And it is said: "ANOVA results reveal that after accounting for body size allometry, not only are there significant inter-population differences in body shape and sexual dimorphism in body shape, but sexual dimorphism also
significantly varies between the two populations. "

How is this function accounting for allometry here?

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Burak,

I´m not sure it is useful to compare examples across packages. Although the authors are (in this case) the same, the purpose of help files is different.

In the example from the geomorph vignette, yes, the term being tested by comparing those two models is the interaction between sex:pop.

The example of RRPP, is illustrating how one might use the lm.rrpp function to evaluate the contribution of sex, population, and their interaction, while accounting for allometry.

Keep in mind that people that use RRPP do not necessarily also use geomorph (but not the other way around, as in reality procD.lm is a wrapper for lm.rrpp). So examples are built with different motivations and purposes. Not sure there is something to understand or compare here.

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Lyna,

The warning message you receive before the error should tip you off to what is wrong.  You are attempting a model lacking replication, probably because certain species are unique in certain locations.  Your combination of variables does not make sense, as a result.  This is why you lose degrees of freedom. This is why interactive terms will not work.

In order to overcome this, you might consider separate single factor analyses, combining your two factors into one, e.g., sp.loc, which maybe has 10 levels, subsetting your data for the cases where you have locations with multiple species, or sticking with the results you got that work, when you did not ask R to consider a model design that is unreasonable.

If none of what I suggest makes sense, it would be imperative to brush up on linear models and understand how design matrices are constructed and used.  If you do something like model.matrix(~ sp * loc), you will see the many columns of 0s that are causing the problem.  This is the problem.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
No, I would not combine them to suggest to others that you used a two-factor model.  I simply meant you could do separate ANOVAs and learn that if you model shape variation on species, 44% of the shape variation is explained.  If you do it for location, 55% of the variation is explained.  But since you have apparently unique species:location situations, you cannot partition the variation.  You cannot say that the 44% variation explained by species is independent of location, or vice versa.

Let's take an extreme example.  You have an analysis that has three species, each located alone in North America, South America, and Africa.  You do two separate analyses for location and species and each looks exactly the same.  They are the same.  Species and location are completely confounded.

Your variables are also confounded.  You simply cannot hope to separate them.  What you could do is combine the variables into one factor, and in pairwise fashion try to infer locational differences.  Maybe species 1 occurs in locations A and B.  Does it have different shapes in those locations?  Maybe species 2 occurs in locations C and D.  Does it differ between locations?  Species 3 only occurs in location E.  There is nothing to compare.

Doing separate ANOVAs on species and location in the above example might reveal both are important but you cannot infer whether it is because of location E or the evolutionary history of species 3, if species 3 is different from the others.  There is no way to deduce that.

I hope that makes sense
Mike

messages.subject: Interpretation of significant Modularity & Integration
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I've been struggling to understand what it means in my data that I have significant Modularity (modularity.test, CR = .9685, p-value = .002) and Integration (Integration.test, r-PLS = 0.935, p-value = 0.001).

I think the reason both can be significant turns on how the tests are structured. Modularity is based on the ratio of within-module covariance and between module covariance. Integration is based on the maximum covariation between subcomponents (i.e., modules). I interpret these tests to mean that a significant result in the Modularity test does not mean there is insignificant between module covariance - there can be, but it is not necessary. A significant result simply means the within-module covariance significantly exceeds the between-module covariance.

Once the within-module covariance part is removed, as it is in the Integration test, one may or may not end up with a significant Integration result.

If this is true, one could reduce the number of LMs in each module to decrease the within-module covariance to the point where modularity is no longer significant, i.e. it is lower than the between module covariance.

I ran some tests of this suggestion. In my original data, I had 2 modules of 24 and 17 LMs (41 total). My smaller dataset had 7 and 6 LMs (13 total). For the smaller dataset, Integration was signficant (r-PLS = .996, p-value = .001), but the Modularity test was insignificant (CR = 1.0414, p-value = 0.082).

Thus, it seems the Modularity test is dependent on the number of inter-module LMs.

Thoughts or comments are appreciated.

Dave

> 24 янв. 2020 г., в 18:00, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> написал(а):
>

> No, I would not combine them to suggest to others that you used a two-factor model.  I simply meant you could do separate ANOVAs and learn that if you model shape variation on species, 44% of the shape variation is explained.  If you do it for location, 55% of the variation is explained.  But since you have apparently unique species:location situations, you cannot partition the variation.  You cannot say that the 44% variation explained by species is independent of location, or vice versa.
>
> Let's take an extreme example.  You have an analysis that has three species, each located alone in North America, South America, and Africa.  You do two separate analyses for location and species and each looks exactly the same.  They are the same.  Species and location are completely confounded.
>
> Your variables are also confounded.  You simply cannot hope to separate them.  What you could do is combine the variables into one factor, and in pairwise fashion try to infer locational differences.  Maybe species 1 occurs in locations A and B.  Does it have different shapes in those locations?  Maybe species 2 occurs in locations C and D.  Does it differ between locations?  Species 3 only occurs in location E.  There is nothing to compare.
>
> Doing separate ANOVAs on species and location in the above example might reveal both are important but you cannot infer whether it is because of location E or the evolutionary history of species 3, if species 3 is different from the others.  There is no way to deduce that.
>
> I hope that makes sense
> Mike

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of significant Modularity & Integration
messages.body_plain:
David,

I previously responded at length on this list about the fact that one can have both integration and modularity in the same dataset. It is possible, both mathematically and structurally to have this occur in the same dataset. Part of my answer touched on what you mentioned: that the tests for each address different components of shape variation and covariation. Please see those prior comments for full details.

As to your landmark removal experiment, I would be far more hesitant on the conclusion made from it. In fact, the test of modularity is not de-facto sensitive to the number of landmarks per module. This was demonstrated via large-scale simulations in the 2016 paper.

Your example however, does more than you think, which is leading to an incorrect conclusion. Removing landmarks not only affects the within-module covariance, but also the between-module covariance. So it is not as simple as ‘remove some landmarks to get rid of the modular signal.’ Also, such ‘point-estimate’ simulations (they are called this because it is on a single dataset) are highly dependent on the structure of the mean shape being used: choose a different structure for this experiment and an entirely different outcome will be found.

For these reasons, large-scale simulations examining trends on many datasets, with many input shapes, are required to claim a method is, or is not, affected by some property.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program

Professor

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://www.eeob.iastate.edu/faculty/adams/

From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of David Thulman
Sent: Friday, January 24, 2020 10:02 AM
To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of significant Modularity & Integration

Hello All,

I've been struggling to understand what it means in my data that I have significant Modularity (modularity.test, CR = .9685, p-value = .002) and Integration (Integration.test, r-PLS = 0.935, p-value = 0.001).

I think the reason both can be significant turns on how the tests are structured. Modularity is based on the ratio of within-module covariance and between module covariance. Integration is based on the maximum covariation between subcomponents (i.e., modules). I interpret these tests to mean that a significant result in the Modularity test does not mean there is insignificant between module covariance - there can be, but it is not necessary. A significant result simply means the within-module covariance significantly exceeds the between-module covariance.

Once the within-module covariance part is removed, as it is in the Integration test, one may or may not end up with a significant Integration result.

If this is true, one could reduce the number of LMs in each module to decrease the within-module covariance to the point where modularity is no longer significant, i.e. it is lower than the between module covariance.

I ran some tests of this suggestion. In my original data, I had 2 modules of 24 and 17 LMs (41 total). My smaller dataset had 7 and 6 LMs (13 total). For the smaller dataset, Integration was signficant (r-PLS = .996, p-value = .001), but the Modularity test was insignificant (CR = 1.0414, p-value = 0.082).

Thus, it seems the Modularity test is dependent on the number of inter-module LMs.

Thoughts or comments are appreciated.

Dave

> > No, I would not combine them to suggest to others that you used a two-factor model.  I simply meant you could do separate ANOVAs and learn that if you model shape variation on species, 44% of the shape variation is explained.  If you do it for location, 55% of the variation is explained.  But since you have apparently unique species:location situations, you cannot partition the variation.  You cannot say that the 44% variation explained by species is independent of location, or vice versa.
> >
> > Let's take an extreme example.  You have an analysis that has three species, each located alone in North America, South America, and Africa.  You do two separate analyses for location and species and each looks exactly the same.  They are the same.  Species and location are completely confounded.
> >
> > Your variables are also confounded.  You simply cannot hope to separate them.  What you could do is combine the variables into one factor, and in pairwise fashion try to infer locational differences.  Maybe species 1 occurs in locations A and B.  Does it have different shapes in those locations?  Maybe species 2 occurs in locations C and D.  Does it differ between locations?  Species 3 only occurs in location E.  There is nothing to compare.
> >
> > Doing separate ANOVAs on species and location in the above example might reveal both are important but you cannot infer whether it is because of location E or the evolutionary history of species 3, if species 3 is different from the others.  There is no way to deduce that.
> >
> > I hope that makes sense
> > Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of significant Modularity & Integration
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the clarifications Dean. They are much appreciated, and your caution about my interpretation is noted.

On Fri, Jan 24, 2020 at 1:01 PM Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

> David,
>
>
> I previously responded at length on this list about the fact that one can have both integration and modularity in the same dataset. It is possible, both mathematically and structurally to have this occur in the same dataset. Part of my answer touched on what you mentioned: that the tests for each address different components of shape variation and covariation. Please see those prior comments for full details.
>
>
>
> As to your landmark removal experiment, I would be far more hesitant on the conclusion made from it. In fact, the test of modularity is not de-facto sensitive to the number of landmarks per module. This was demonstrated via large-scale simulations in the 2016 paper.
>
>
>
> Your example however, does more than you think, which is leading to an incorrect conclusion. Removing landmarks not only affects the within-module covariance, but also the between-module covariance. So it is not as simple as ‘remove some landmarks to get rid of the modular signal.’ Also, such ‘point-estimate’ simulations (they are called this because it is on a single dataset) are highly dependent on the structure of the mean shape being used: choose a different structure for this experiment and an entirely different outcome will be found.
>
>
>
> For these reasons, large-scale simulations examining trends on many datasets, with many input shapes, are required to claim a method is, or is not, affected by some property.
>
>
>
> Dean
>
>
>
> Dr. Dean C. Adams
>
> Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program
>
> Professor
>
> Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology
>
> Iowa State University
>
> https://www.eeob.iastate.edu/faculty/adams/
>
> phone: 515-294-3834
>
>
>
> From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of David Thulman
> Sent: Friday, January 24, 2020 10:02 AM
> To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Interpretation of significant Modularity & Integration
>
>
>
> Hello All,
>
>
>
> I've been struggling to understand what it means in my data that I have significant Modularity (modularity.test, CR = .9685, p-value = .002) and Integration (Integration.test, r-PLS = 0.935, p-value = 0.001).
>
>
>
> I think the reason both can be significant turns on how the tests are structured. Modularity is based on the ratio of within-module covariance and between module covariance. Integration is based on the maximum covariation between subcomponents (i.e., modules). I interpret these tests to mean that a significant result in the Modularity test does not mean there is insignificant between module covariance - there can be, but it is not necessary. A significant result simply means the within-module covariance significantly exceeds the between-module covariance.
>
>
>
> Once the within-module covariance part is removed, as it is in the Integration test, one may or may not end up with a significant Integration result.
>
>
>
> If this is true, one could reduce the number of LMs in each module to decrease the within-module covariance to the point where modularity is no longer significant, i.e. it is lower than the between module covariance.
>
>
>
> I ran some tests of this suggestion. In my original data, I had 2 modules of 24 and 17 LMs (41 total). My smaller dataset had 7 and 6 LMs (13 total). For the smaller dataset, Integration was signficant (r-PLS = .996, p-value = .001), but the Modularity test was insignificant (CR = 1.0414, p-value = 0.082).
>
>
>
> Thus, it seems the Modularity test is dependent on the number of inter-module LMs.
>
>
>
> Thoughts or comments are appreciated.
>
>
>
> Dave

> > > > No, I would not combine them to suggest to others that you used a two-factor model.  I simply meant you could do separate ANOVAs and learn that if you model shape variation on species, 44% of the shape variation is explained.  If you do it for location, 55% of the variation is explained.  But since you have apparently unique species:location situations, you cannot partition the variation.  You cannot say that the 44% variation explained by species is independent of location, or vice versa.
> > > >
> > > > Let's take an extreme example.  You have an analysis that has three species, each located alone in North America, South America, and Africa.  You do two separate analyses for location and species and each looks exactly the same.  They are the same.  Species and location are completely confounded.
> > > >
> > > > Your variables are also confounded.  You simply cannot hope to separate them.  What you could do is combine the variables into one factor, and in pairwise fashion try to infer locational differences.  Maybe species 1 occurs in locations A and B.  Does it have different shapes in those locations?  Maybe species 2 occurs in locations C and D.  Does it differ between locations?  Species 3 only occurs in location E.  There is nothing to compare.
> > > >
> > > > Doing separate ANOVAs on species and location in the above example might reveal both are important but you cannot infer whether it is because of location E or the evolutionary history of species 3, if species 3 is different from the others.  There is no way to deduce that.

messages.subject_clean: Picking between Mahalanobis and Procrustes Distances
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm working with geometric morphometrics for my thesis project. I am looking at the differences in head shape between species within a species complex. During my research, I came across both Mahalanobis and Procrustes Distances. For those who have done their analysis, which distance did you decide to pick and why? How did you come to that decision? I've sat down with professors to break down the meaning behind the two distances, and why they are different in an effort to determine which one to use for my project, but I'm curious on what others have done and how they came to the decision which to use.

Thanks!

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Picking between Mahalanobis and Procrustes Distances
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Picking between Mahalanobis and Procrustes Distances
messages.body_plain:
Sara,

Procrustes distance is simply the Euclidean distance between shapes in tangent space. Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance standardized by within-group covariation.  As you noted, both are used in the literature to describe differences in shape, and both are appropriate under different circumstances. If one wishes to describe the ‘raw’ shape difference: Procrustes distance is preferred. It is also preferred if one wishes to perform a permutation test to see if group means are significantly different from one another (see below). However, if one wishes to account for the direction of within-group variation in their interpretation of distance, one would use Mahalanobis distance.

To visualize the difference, think of three points. #1 is at the origin, #2 is at 0,2 on the X-axis and #3 is at 2,0 on the Y-axis. Both #2 and #3 are equidistant from #1 using Procrustes distance. Now add one more thing: the within-group covariation. Say it is a horizontal ellipse, centered at the origin (point #1). One standard deviation of our distribution makes an ellipse that bisects the X-axis at +/-1, and bisects the Y-axis at +/- 0.5.  Two stds bisect X at +/-2 and Y at +/-1. Now, because the within-group variation aligns with the X-axis in our example, the Mahalanobis distance between #1 & #2 will be smaller than between #1 & #3.   That is seen in the plot: #2 is only 1 std away along X, while #3 is 2 std away along Y. In other words, it is ‘easier’ for differences to accumulate in directions that coincide with the main axis of within-group variation. This is reflected in Mahalanobis distance.

Now, if one wishes to use the distances in a statistical test via permutation, say to determine whether two shapes are different, Procrustes distance is preferred. The reason is that permuting objects into groups and repeatedly calculating D.Mahal will change both the expected distances between groups (the ‘numerator’ of D.Mahal) and the within-group variation (the ‘denominator’ of D.Mahal). Thus, one does not know whether a significant value means the groups are further away than expected, or have less pooled within-group variation than expected. That is undesirable.

By contrast, using Procrustes distance, it is unambiguous: a significant result means that the groups are further away than expected.

Hope this helps,

Dean

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] plot.mshape is missing
messages.body_plain:
Dave,

As an S3 plot generic, the function is not a top level geomorph function. It is supposed to work just using plot(). The “mshape” class of the object informs R that plot = plot.mshape. You can use the function directly, as if to override the S3 generic designation with:

geomorph:::plot.mshape(XX)

The function is not missing, it is just an internal function that can only be called by a class match.

Mike
